children: is seeking a two-year wage freeze, greater working-hour flexibility and the removal of an employee bonus as the German automaker prepares for contentious labour negotiations with unions amid an escalating cost-cutting drive, Reuters reported on Thursday.

The company also wants to reopen discussions on the 35-hour work week, potentially allowing it to require employees to work longer hours without additional pay. The proposals have drawn strong opposition from IG Metall, whose chief negotiator Thorsten Groeger warned of a “tough, bitter, and exhausting conflict.”
employees are scheduled to begin Tuesday in Emden, Germany. The dispute could lead to strikes around the turn of the year, with workers already threatening industrial action from January.
The confrontation comes as Chief Executive Officer Oliver Blume pushes ahead with a restructuring programme that includes plans to cut 100,000 jobs.

labour tensions reflect broader challenges facing Germany's automotive industry, including weak demand, growing competition from Chinese manufacturers and pressure to reduce domestic production costs. Similar disputes over working hours are also emerging at Mercedes-Benz and other German industrial companies.
